# Results — Study 462 (Rising Wedge)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a rising
wedge is bearish: price breaks down through the rising support line, so short the break** —
encoded as a mechanical rule. Pivots are confirmed fractals (k = 10, with a 10-bar confirmation
lag); at every bar a support line is fit through the last confirmed swing lows and a resistance
line through the last confirmed swing highs; the pattern qualifies as a **rising wedge** when
both lines rise, support rises faster (converging), and the lines have not yet crossed. A
**short** fires on the first close below the rising support, entered at the **next close** (one
documented lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day **short** return (a price fall is a
gain). Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every
number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **340** mechanical rising-wedge support-break shorts pooled across the 5 tapes (k = 10) |
| Timing / costs | confirmed-fractal pivots usable only **+10 bars** later; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per break |

> **Short convention.** The rising wedge is a *bearish* pattern, so the trade is a **short**:
> the forward return is `-(P_{t+H}/P_t − 1)`. A positive number means the short made money
> (price fell); a negative number means price *rose* after the "bearish" break and the short
> lost. The Signal axis is **break-down short vs a drift-matched random-entry baseline** (also
> shorted), the only honest test on an upward-drifting tape.

## The signal — wedge-break short vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift working
*against* a short); the **Welch break-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = break − random.

| horizon | n | short | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (break−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 340 | −6.9 bps | 44% | −0.62 | −0.3 bps | **−6.6 bps** | −8.9 bps | −0.33 | 0.741 |
| 10-day | 340 | −41.6 bps | 39% | −2.43 | −24.3 bps | **−17.4 bps** | −43.6 bps | −0.68 | 0.495 |
| 20-day | 340 | −93.7 bps | 36% | −3.47 | −59.3 bps | **−34.3 bps** | −95.7 bps | −0.96 | 0.339 |
| 60-day | 339 | −325.5 bps | 27% | −6.03 | −240.5 bps | **−85.0 bps** | −327.5 bps | −1.48 | 0.140 |

Read it carefully. The wedge-break short **loses money at every horizon** (short return is
negative throughout — i.e. price *rose* after the supposedly bearish break). The big negative
one-sample *t*'s (**−3.47** at 20 days, **−6.03** at 60) are **pure beta working against the
short**: a short on an upward-drifting index inherits the drift as a loss. Against the
**drift-matched random baseline** (also shorted, so it eats the same drift), the wedge break is
*even worse* — Δ = −6.6 / −17.4 / −34.3 / −85.0 bps at 5/10/20/60 days. The break-minus-random
difference **never clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** (max |Welch *t*| = 1.48 at 60 days,
*p* = 0.140). **The rising wedge does not forecast a downside break — if anything it precedes a
relief rally.**

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the break-down short underperforms random almost everywhere

| ticker | entries | short | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (break−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 74 | −100.2 bps | −1.79 | −72.5 bps | **−27.7 bps** |
| QQQ | 71 | −139.6 bps | −2.08 | −114.9 bps | **−24.6 bps** |
| IWM | 67 | −37.1 bps | −0.52 | +28.9 bps | **−66.0 bps** |
| DIA | 74 | −54.4 bps | −1.16 | −59.0 bps | **+4.6 bps** |
| GLD | 54 | −148.3 bps | −1.91 | −77.7 bps | **−70.5 bps** |

Only **DIA** edges out a tiny positive delta (+4.6 bps); in 4 of 5 names the famous "bearish"
break *underperforms* a random short. No coherent cross-sectional edge — the hallmark of a
pattern that carries no information beyond the tape's drift.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the support slope, nothing changes

The decisive "does the wedge geometry matter?" test: keep the break *cadence* (a short fires
only where a wedge was active) but replace the fitted rising support with a random-but-plausible
line (slope/level drawn from the empirical support distribution), so the geometry becomes
nonsense. If price genuinely respected *this specific rising line*, the scramble would collapse
the result.

| test | observed break-down 20d short | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY slope-scramble | −100.2 bps | **0.248** | 500 |

**25% of scrambled-geometry breaks match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.248). The fitted rising
support carries no special information — a nonsense line does about as well. "The rising wedge
forecasts the break-down" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real break-down

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* rising-wedge break-down (knob `edge`: a clean rising,
narrowing build-up followed by a brief downward resolution near the apex), the same short rule
behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there", not a
dead detector.

| planted edge | n | short | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no break-down) | 37 | −67.6 bps | 41% | −0.84 |
| **0.50** (real planted break-down) | 11 | +725.6 bps | 100% | **+4.88** |

With no planted break-down the control sits near *t* ≈ 0 (a fair coin, no false positive); a
real planted break-down lights up at *t* = +4.88 with a 100% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The wedge-break short does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (break − random = −6.6 / −17.4 / −34.3 / −85.0 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the break-vs-random
  Welch *t* never clears 2, max |1.48| at 60 days, *p* = 0.140). The big one-sample *t*'s
  (20-day −3.47, 60-day −6.03) are pure beta working against a short on an upward-drifting tape.
  The "bearish" break is, on the real tape, followed by a relief *rally*.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is nothing to deploy: shorting the break loses money outright,
  and underperforms even a random short once the drift is matched. Costs only deepen the hole.
  No edge to scale.
- **"Does the wedge forecast a downside break?" — BUSTED.** The slope-scramble placebo leaves
  the result intact (*p* = 0.248): nonsense support lines do about as well as the real fitted
  one, so the specific rising-wedge geometry carries no forecasting information. The rising wedge
  is a descriptive after-the-fact label, not a bearish forecast.
